newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman supported by 36 percent of Croatian voters.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman supported by 36 percent of Croatian voters.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman won a mandate to rule Croatia for another five years with the support of just 36 percent of the electorate.

At only 57 percent, the turnout in Sunday's election was one of the lowest since 1990 when Croatia, then a republic of former Yugoslavia, broke with its communist past to organise the first democratic and free election in half a century.
With 90 percent of the count complete, he had just over 60 percent of the vote.
"Tudjman proved yet again that he is a master of turning the minority into a majority," political analyst Davor Gjenero said.

The 75-year-old president won his second full term in office, fortifying his iron grip on power following the victory of his ruling HDZ party in the 1995 parliamentary election and its landslide in April's municipal poll.
Analysts, independent observers and opposition candidates blamed the low turnout on apathy.
Sunny weather may also have affected voters, a diplomat said. Many Croatians leave Zagreb for the seaside at weekends.
Most pre-election polls showed Tudjman would win in the first round with 55-60 percent of votes.

"This was a very dull election, as the result was known in advance," said Davor Butkovic, editor of the independent weekly Globus. "There was no drama, no passion, no uncertainty and no issues, so people asked themselves 'why bother?'."
Vlado Gotovac, the presidential candidate of nine centrist parties, who came third, winning only 18 percent of the vote, blamed his bad showing on the low turnout.

"The most important thing about this election was the huge abstention of voters, which shows that a large portion of the electorate is not interested in any election," Gotovac said after the first results were published.
"It is an expression of some desperation, resignation at least, a disbelief that there can be any changes."
